title: The ants that guard a tree
teaches: What a mutualism is, what each partner pays, and how cheaters threaten it

blocks.text: Thomas Belt was a British mining engineer who spent four years from 1868 to 1872 running gold mines in Chontales, Nicaragua. In his spare time he watched animals, and in 1874 he published *The Naturalist in Nicaragua*, which Darwin called the best of all natural history journals. One of its puzzles was a small tree, the bullhorn acacia.

The bullhorn acacia has pairs of large, swollen thorns shaped like a bull's horns. Each pair is hollow, and in almost every tree the hollows were full of small, fierce ants that stung anyone who brushed the branches. The tree seemed to be looking after them. At the base of each leaf stalk it had little cups that oozed sweet nectar[^extrafloral-nectaries]. And at the tip of each tiny leaflet sat a yellow-orange bead, rich in protein and fat, that the ants picked off and carried home to feed their larvae. These are now called **Beltian bodies**, after him.

Belt guessed what the tree got in return. The ants swarmed out to attack anything that touched it, and in particular they drove off the leaf-cutting ants that stripped other trees in the area bare. The ants, he wrote, were “a standing army for the plant”. It was a good story, though some prominent naturalists doubted that the tree needed them[^wheeler-doubt]. Nobody tested it properly for ninety years.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The bullhorn acacia houses ants in hollow thorns and feeds them nectar and protein-rich Beltian bodies.
In 1874 Thomas Belt guessed the ants were the tree's guards.

blocks.text: In the early 1960s Daniel Janzen, a graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley, went to the lowlands of eastern Mexico, where bullhorn acacias grow in old fields and along roadsides. Their ants were *Pseudomyrmex ferrugineus*, slender, fast and stinging. He spent months watching them. They patrolled the tree day and night. They attacked insects that landed on it and bit and stung the muzzles of browsing animals. They also chewed off any vine or branch of another plant that touched the acacia, and cleared a ring of bare ground around its base.

Then he did what Belt hadn't. On some acacias he removed the ants, by cutting off the shoots whose thorns held the colony or by spraying them with insecticide, and kept them off. He left other acacias with their ants and compared the two over the following year.

blocks.caption: A young bullhorn acacia over a year, with and without its ants. A model, shaped after Janzen's results.
blocks.task: Guess, then take the ants away and run a year

blocks.text: The trees without ants did badly. Beetles, caterpillars and bugs chewed them, the new shoots grew less than a sixth as much, vines and neighbouring shrubs grew over and shaded them, and over a year more than half of them died. The trees with ants grew fast and stayed clean. Janzen published the results in 1966. Belt's guess was right: without its ants, the bullhorn acacia can barely survive.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The ants attack insects and browsers and cut away vines and nearby plants.
When Janzen removed the ants, acacias were eaten and overgrown, and many died.

blocks.text: A relationship in which two species each do better because of the other is called a **mutualism**. It is easy to think of mutualism as kindness, but neither partner is being kind. Each is paying a price for something it gets.

The tree pays in food and housing: the sugar in the nectar, the protein and fat in thousands of Beltian bodies, and the tissue in the swollen thorns. All of that could have gone into growing. What it gets is protection, worth far more. The ants pay in work and risk: they spend their lives on patrol, and they are tied to one tree, unable to live anywhere else. What they get is a home and a steady food supply that no other ant can take from them.

blocks.caption: The tree's side of the bargain: how well it grows for what it pays its ants. Paying too little gets no guards; paying too much costs more than the guards save. A model.
blocks.task: Raise the share of cheating colonies until paying the ants hardly pays

blocks.text: Like any bargain, it has a best price. Pay too little and the colony stays small and the guard is thin. Pay too much and the tree spends more than the protection saves. Ant acacias seem to have given up other defences: in the 1970s David Seigler, John Ebinger and Janzen found that, unlike many other acacias, they lack the cyanide-making chemicals that make leaves bitter and poisonous to eat[^cyanide]. Their protection is the ants.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A **mutualism** is a relationship in which both species do better.
Each side pays: the tree in food and housing, the ants in work and risk.
The trade holds when each gains more than it pays.

blocks.text: Any deal in which one side pays in advance invites cheating. In 1975 Janzen described another ant, *Pseudomyrmex nigropilosus*, that also lives in bullhorn acacias. It moves into vacant thorns, eats the nectar and Beltian bodies, and raises its young. But it doesn't patrol and runs away rather than attack when the tree is disturbed. It takes the tree's pay and does none of the work. Janzen called it “a parasite of a mutualism”.

Cheaters like this one are kept rare in part by the guards themselves. A colony of *P. ferrugineus* that finds another colony on its tree attacks and kills it, and the true guards grow larger colonies and take over most trees as they mature. But in the trade figure you can see what would happen if cheaters became common. The tree's return for paying falls, and when most colonies cheat, paying hardly pays at all. A tree that stopped paying would lose little, and the whole partnership could unravel.

Many mutualisms have ways of punishing cheats. The yucca moth is the yucca's only pollinator: the female gathers pollen, carries it to another flower, packs it onto the stigma, and lays her eggs in the flower's ovary, where her caterpillars will eat some of the seeds. A moth that lays too many eggs in one flower would take too many seeds, and yuccas tend to drop flowers loaded with too many eggs, killing the caterpillars inside. The plant pays for pollination, but not any price.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A cheater takes a mutualism's reward without paying its cost.
Mutualisms last when cheaters are kept rare, for instance by the partners punishing them.

blocks.text: The acacia and its ants look exotic, but mutualisms are all around. The grey-green crust on a rock or a fencepost is a lichen, which is a fungus and an alga (or a cyanobacterium) living as one: the alga makes sugar from sunlight, the fungus holds water and minerals and gives the alga a place to live. Most bees and many flies, moths, birds and bats are paid in nectar and pollen to carry pollen between flowers. Cleaner fish on coral reefs eat parasites off larger fish, which come to their “stations” and hold still to be cleaned.

Some of the most important are underground. The roots of most land plants are joined to fungi whose threads spread through the soil, gathering water and phosphorus for the plant in return for sugar[^mycorrhizae]. Peas, beans and clover carry bacteria in small swellings on their roots that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form the plant can use; the plant pays them in sugar too. The Botany course meets both, and the bacteria answer a question farmers had wondered about since Roman times, when writers already advised sowing beans to enrich a field: why crops grow better after beans.

Lesson 7 showed how predators can hold a community together. Mutualisms do it too, in a different way. Lose the bullhorn acacia's ants and you lose the acacia, because the insects and neighbouring plants that the ants kept back overwhelm it. Remove the fungi from a forest's soil and most of its trees grow badly. Much of what lives together depends on who eats whom, and just as much on who helps whom.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Lichens, pollinators, cleaner fish, root fungi and the bacteria in bean roots are all mutualisms.
Mutualisms can hold communities together as much as predators can.

blocks.caption: Six questions on mutualism
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Janzen removed the ants from young bullhorn acacias. What happened to them?
choices: They were eaten by insects and overgrown by vines, and many died
They grew faster, saving the food they had fed the ants
items.why: The ants were the tree's defence. Without them, plant-eaters and neighbouring plants took over.

items.ask: What does the bullhorn acacia pay its ants?
choices: Nectar, protein-rich Beltian bodies and hollow thorns to live in
Nothing: the ants live there by chance
items.why: The tree feeds and houses the ants; all of that could otherwise have gone into growing.

items.ask: An ant lives in acacia thorns and eats the tree's food but never attacks anything. What is it?
items.why: It takes the reward without providing the service, as Janzen's Pseudomyrmex nigropilosus does.

items.ask: In the trade figure, why does the tree's growth fall again when it pays its ants a lot?
choices: The extra food costs more than the extra protection is worth
items.why: Protection levels off once the colony is big enough, but the cost keeps rising. Every bargain has a best price.

items.ask: Yuccas tend to drop flowers in which moths have laid too many eggs. What does that do?
choices: It punishes moths that would take too many seeds
items.why: The caterpillars inside die with the dropped flower, so moths that overcharge for pollination leave fewer young. That keeps cheating rare.

items.ask: A lichen is a fungus and an alga growing together. What does each give the other?
choices: The alga makes sugar; the fungus holds water and minerals and shelters the alga
The fungus makes sugar; the alga holds water
items.why: Each does what the other can't: the alga photosynthesises, the fungus gathers and holds water and minerals.

summary: **Bullhorn acacias house and feed fierce ants.** Hollow thorns, nectar, and protein-rich Beltian bodies, as Thomas Belt described in 1874.
**The ants are the tree's guards.** They attack insects and browsers and cut away vines and nearby plants.
**Janzen removed the ants in the 1960s.** The acacias were eaten and overgrown, and many died.
**A mutualism is a trade.** Each side pays a cost and gains more than it pays.
**Every bargain has a best price.** Too little pay gets no guards; too much costs more than the guards save.
**Cheaters take the reward without the work.** If they become common, paying stops paying and the partnership can unravel.
**Partners often punish cheats.** Yuccas drop flowers overloaded with yucca moth eggs.
**Mutualisms are everywhere.** Lichens, pollinators, cleaner fish, root fungi and the bacteria in bean roots.

extrafloral-nectaries.title: Extrafloral nectaries
extrafloral-nectaries.text: Nectar glands outside a flower, on leaf stalks, stems or bracts, are called **extrafloral nectaries**. Flowers make nectar to draw pollinators; extrafloral nectaries draw bodyguards, usually ants or parasitoid wasps.

wheeler-doubt.title: Scientists who thought Belt was wrong
wheeler-doubt.text: For decades several leading biologists dismissed Belt's idea as sentimental storytelling. The great American ant specialist William Morton Wheeler argued in 1913 that the acacias got no real benefit and the ants were simply parasites taking free food and shelter. Only when Janzen ran a controlled removal experiment in the 1960s was the argument settled.

cyanide.title: Cyanide in acacia leaves
cyanide.text: Many acacias that do not keep ants store **cyanogenic glycosides** in their leaves. When a caterpillar or browser chews a leaf, enzymes mix with these compounds and release hydrogen cyanide, which is both bitter and poisonous.

mycorrhizae.title: Mycorrhizae and root nodules
mycorrhizae.text: The partnership between plant roots and soil fungi is a **mycorrhiza** (from the Greek for "fungus-root"), and more than four fifths of land plant species form one. The bacteria inside the root nodules of peas, beans and clover are **rhizobia**.
